We introduce XForecast, a benchmark and competition for news-grounded financial forecasting, where the task is to predict stock price movements four weeks ahead using both historical price data and paired news signals. XForecast combines stock price data with curated financial text generated using FinTexTS, a multimodal dataset generation method. It covers 100 large-cap stocks from 2019--2023, with training on 2019--2022 and evaluation on 2023. To better evaluate models that leverage textual signals, we adopt a weighted hit rate metric that places greater emphasis on instances where news information is expected to have stronger influence. The XForecast Challenge, hosted on Kaggle as part of KDD 2026 Finance Day, aims to benchmark methods for integrating financial TS and textual information.

title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
summary: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.

title: WildTrace: Evaluating Training Data Detection in Realistic Large-Scale LLM Post-Training
summary: Although post-training significantly enhances model performance, the use of massive undisclosed data raises concerns about benchmark contamination and copyright infringement. This drives growing interest in training data detection for post-trained models. Existing evaluations for training data detection often leverage benchmarks constructed post hoc, which can introduce distribution shifts. Alternatively, controlled evaluations rely on small-scale training setups that diverge from realistic post-training settings. As a result, their reported performance may not faithfully reflect the effectiveness of detection methods in real-world scenarios. To this end, we introduce \textsc{\method}, a reliable benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods in realistic, large-scale post-training settings. Built on a multi-stage pipeline, \method\space encompasses stage-specific models throughout the post-training lifecycle, spanning SFT, DPO, and RL. To perform a reliable evaluation, we construct model-specific evaluation sets across four diverse tasks, featuring distribution-matched members and non-members with verifiable membership labels. Our results reveal that even the best-performing method achieves an average AUC of only 0.529 on our benchmark, which approaches random-guessing level (0.5). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluation protocols can significantly affect measured detection performance. These findings highlight the significant potential for developing effective, practical, and robust detection methods under realistic scenarios.

title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks
comment: 20 pages (10 pages main text), 11 figures (6 figures main text), NeurIPS 2026
summary: A fruitful approach towards understanding generalization in machine learning involves characterizing how models separate generalizable structure from idiosyncratic or even corrupted features of training data. Fisher information has emerged as a diagnostic tool for this separation, leveraging loss geometry to distinguish generalization from memorization. Here we investigate this connection in vision models trained on CIFAR-10 with controlled noise that can be learned only through memorization. We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization, and we investigate how this decoupling presents differentially across layers. We show that the same phenomena are present in small transformers trained to solve a synthetic in-context learning task, and are reproduced in closed form in a simple, analytically solvable linear model. Our results reveal that Fisher information captures aspects of the geometric structure underlying how neural networks allocate capacity between generalization and memorization.

title: When Participant Disjoint Validation Is Not Enough to Establish Generalization in Parkinson's Gait Classification
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Includes supplementary analyses integrated into the appendices
summary: Participant-disjoint cross-validation prevents direct participant overlap, but it may still produce optimistic estimates when acquisition site and diagnosis are structurally dependent. We examined Parkinson's disease classification using 159 pressure-walkway summary features from 133 WearGait-PD participants, including 65 participants with Parkinson's disease and 68 controls. The cohort was non-factorial: two sites contained only one diagnostic group, whereas VA-Seattle was the only site containing both groups. In repeated participant-level nested cross-validation, site alone achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.955 plus or minus 0.003, exceeding the gait-feature model (0.882 plus or minus 0.014). Under the evaluated logistic-regression pipelines, adding gait features to site, age, and sex produced no measurable improvement in pooled discrimination. More site-controlled evaluations produced lower and imprecise estimates: VA-Seattle same-site AUC was 0.668 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.477 to 0.836), and the JHOC + Bayview-to-VA-Seattle transport stress test achieved 0.576 (0.375 to 0.770). Supporting within-diagnosis site-prediction and site-conditioned permutation analyses showed that the gait representation retained substantial acquisition-site structure. These findings indicate that participant-disjoint pooled validation did not isolate disease-related discrimination from site-associated variation. They encourage careful examination of site-label dependence and, where possible, support for pooled results through within-site or independent validation before broader claims are made about generalization across institutions.

title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Agentic AI for Biological Discovery
summary: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.

title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos
summary:
Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics.
  We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development.
  Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.

title: Reflected Proximal Dynamics for Accelerated High-Accuracy Log-Concave Sampling
summary: We study sampling from $π(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ is $α$-strongly convex and $β$-smooth with condition number $κ=β/α$. For this problem, the proximal sampler preserves the target exactly and recovers overdamped Langevin dynamics in the small-step limit, but its Gaussian resampling step discards directional information. Underdamped Langevin dynamics retains such information through momentum to accelerate exploration, motivating a proximal construction that combines target preservation with directional persistence. We introduce \textit{reflected proximal dynamics}, which combines proximal sampling with an exact reflection of the auxiliary variable, conditional kinetic motion, and controlled refreshment. We develop two realizations: a flux-resampled underdamped half-turn and a persistent-momentum quarter-turn. From a warm start with constant $χ^2$ divergence, both methods achieve total variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde O(\sqrtκd^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. We further remove the supplied warm-start assumption by combining either sampler with existing posterior samplers in a proximal initialization stage with an optimized coarse step size. Accounting for both initialization and sampling yields $\widetilde O(κ^{6/7}d^{1/4})$ expected oracle queries. In both regimes, the dependence on the target accuracy $\varepsilon$ is $\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)$, making reflected proximal dynamics a promising framework for accelerated high-accuracy log-concave sampling.

title: Spectral Considerations on Unsupervised Time-domain EEG Representation Learning with Deep Networks
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive, scalable source of quantitative biomarkers for the early diagnosis of brain disorders, and deep representation learning has become a powerful paradigm for extracting information-rich latent features from raw signals. However, neural networks tend to under-represent high-frequency information, a concern that is especially acute for EEG given its oscillatory nature and characteristic $1/f^χ$ power decay, which risks masking disease-relevant high-frequency signatures. In this study, we systematically investigate the spectral constraints of unsupervised time-domain feature extraction across three autoencoder architectures (LSTMVAE, VAEEG, Transformer) and a state-of-the-art EEG foundation model. Using synthetic experiments and empirical validation, we show that while autoencoders capture macro-scale shifts such as alpha slowing, they remain biased against higher frequencies due to a magnitude-driven masking effect induced by the Mean Squared Error loss under 1/f-decaying spectra. Increasing latent dimensionality mitigates this attenuation but sacrifices latent compactness and generative stability. We argue that, as the field advances toward large-scale foundation-level feature extractors, it is imperative to move beyond simple time-domain reconstruction and to integrate spectral-domain loss terms and gradient-balancing techniques, so that the subtle high-frequency transients critical for diagnosing complex brain disorders are preserved in the latent representation.

title: Error Correction in Trained TTT Layers
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Code and saved results included as ancillary material and at https://github.com/aliceyh7/ttt-error-correction
summary: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.

title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
comment: 52 pages. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. Survey Certification. Reviewed on OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=P6e5IC4gPe
summary: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.

title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
summary:
Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension.
  In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements.
  We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/δ))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/δ))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.

title: SLDBench v2: Active Scaling Law Discovery
summary: Scaling laws predict large-model performance from small experiments, but finding a reliable law itself requires costly experiments. SLDBench tests whether language-model agents can discover scaling laws when all experimental results are given upfront. We introduce SLDBench v2 with two extensions. First, we expand the corpus from 8 to 127 scenarios spanning language-model pretraining, downstream performance, and vision-language transfer, and select 30 challenging scenarios on which a reference power-law fit reaches $R^2 \le 0.8$; they represent at least $1.09 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs of source-reported training compute. Second, we introduce active scaling law discovery: an agent chooses which experiments to run, pays each one's recorded cost (e.g., training FLOPs), and revises its law as outcomes arrive, and is scored on the same hidden extrapolation targets as in the passive setting. Across 8 frontier agent systems, median $R^2$ drops from 0.72-0.75 (passive) to 0.24-0.57 (active), and prediction error rises 1.5-4.7 times, depending on the system. Agents favor cheap experiments, spending 8-44% of the full-pool cost on average; low-cost acquisition can yield strong predictions, but cheap purchases also leave experimental conditions needed for extrapolation unobserved. Experimental planning thus remains a key open challenge for agents that assist model development in the prevailing AI-for-AI study.

title: BehaviorFormer: Discovering Behavioral Patterns via Clusterable Next-Token Prediction
comment: Accepted at IEEE Conference on Games 2026
summary: Discovering behavioral patterns in open-ended games is challenging due to the lack of clear objectives or ground-truth annotations. In this work, we extend a next-token prediction Transformer with the deep clustering algorithm DCSS to learn meaningful representations with well-separated clusters. In a controlled Minecraft session with 26 players, the method discovers 23 distinct behavioral patterns that generalize across the studied players, further refining structures present in self-supervised representations into clearly separable clusters. We group the clusters into seven interpretable categories covering stationary, roaming, travel, mining, base work, logging, and farming behavior.

title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
summary: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.

title: Rescuing Points Trapped Inside Incorrect Decision Regions: A target for Evaluating and Improving Forward-Forward Learning
summary: Forward-Forward learning replaces end-to-end backpropagation with local, layer-wise training objectives. Its variants are evaluated primarily by classification accuracy, often measured with linear probes trained on their representations. We show that this evaluation can over-credit the learning method: a linear probe on the representations of an untrained convolutional neural network already reaches accuracy well above chance. Moreover, a single accuracy value does not reveal which datapoints become correctly classified after training and which remain misclassified. To examine what learning contributes beyond the random, untrained baseline, we present an analysis methodology built on the Boundary Proximity Index (BPI), a multiclass margin normalized by a class-centroid reference. We apply our analysis to seven Forward-Forward variants and related layer-local methods and find that initially misclassified points near the probe's decision boundary generally have higher rescue rates than those farther inside incorrect decision regions. Rescue rates vary substantially across methods, with some correcting a substantial fraction of these deeply embedded points. Together, these analyses offer a way to evaluate representation learning beyond accuracy and identify the rescue of points far inside incorrect decision regions as a target for improving local learning methods.

title: DWI Connectome-based Sex Classification in Young using Supervised Variational Autoencoder
summary: During adolescence, significant changes in brain development are influenced by hormonal changes that impact both the body and the brain. This study presents sex classification in 787 young adults having age range of 15-25 years using Diffusion-weighted (DWI) structural connectome, focusing on 82 Desikan-Killiany atlas ROIs. A supervised variational autoencoder (SVAE) is used to extract latent space features from DWI connectome data. Although several studies explored differences in brain structure and function between sexes, the main contribution of this study lies in incorporating SVAE to learn a compact, regularized latent representation for the task of sex classification. Initial exploratory data analysis shows that these features can capture the differences in sex-specific latent space patterns. Subsequently, the learned latent space SVAE features are fed to different ML models for sex classification. Among the considered ML classifiers, the multi-layer perceptron yields the highest accuracy of 80% in classifying sex. This demonstrates the effectiveness of SVAE in learning compact, informative representations from DWI connectome for sex classification. The present work highlights the potential of using DWI brain connectomics and deep learning to differentiate sex, paving the way for future research on diverse populations that may include transgender individuals, to better understand sex-related variations in brain structure.

title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].

title: Sampling from Neural Operator Priors to Solve Partial Differential Equations
summary: Guided sampling with sparse observations and PDE residuals has recently been combined with neural operator priors to solve partial differential equations in function space, their natural setting. We pair such a prior with pseudo-bootstrap sequential Monte Carlo (pBS SMC), a guided sampling framework that accommodates proposals without tractable densities, and introduce a new proposal by adapting the DPM++ algorithm to the guidance setting. Across five benchmark PDE systems this proposal attains the best error--time trade-off at every step count tested, and wrapping it in pBS gives the lowest error on most inverse-problem settings, with the largest gains when few sampling steps are used.

title: Learning $ω$-Powered Conditional Distributions with Importance-Weighted Flow Matching
summary: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) with guidance scale $γ$ is commonly motivated by the $ω$-powered conditional distribution obtained by setting $ω=γ$, but CFG does not, in general, sample from this distribution exactly. We study whether the powered target can instead be learned explicitly. We introduce Importance-Weighted Conditional Flow Matching (IW-CFM), which reweights conditional flow-matching examples using density ratios obtained from frozen conditional and unconditional flow models. With exact normalized weights, the resulting objective has the same gradient as flow matching on the powered target; in practice, we use self-normalized estimation and a regularized empirical approximation for high-dimensional data. On synthetic distributions, IW-CFM recovers analytical powered targets for which numerically matched CFG, $γ=ω$, exhibits a visible mismatch. On ImageNet, an amortized lightweight corrector achieves better alignment than fixed- and matched-guidance CFG with the corresponding weighted and filtered reference distributions. We additionally present an exploratory CLIP analysis of powered-density rankings on real ImageNet data. Aggregate shifts across selected prompt-specific contrasts coexist with heterogeneous classwise responses, including nonmonotonic trajectories. These results provide a practical route for studying and approximating model-defined powered conditional distributions.

title: Resample the Answer: Where to Spend Test-Time Compute in Recursive Reasoning
summary: Recursive reasoning models such as the Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) iteratively refine two latent states: an answer state y, decoded into the output, and a reasoning state z, which is never decoded. Many of their failures have been attributed to bad basins, regions of latent space that trap the recursion on wrong answers. Recent test-time approaches perturb y, z or both to recover these failures, but the impact of this choice on performance, test-time compute efficiency and scaling properties remains unclear. Through controlled experiments on TRM, we find that a failed trajectory carries its failure in its answer state. At equal compute, in depth and in width, resampling y recovers more failures than any perturbation of z we tested, and the performance gap widens as the test-time compute budget grows. Our approach, Gated Answer Resampling (GAR), pairs this resampling of the answer state with the model's own halting head and restarts only the puzzles that the head rejects. With at most 64 restarts per puzzle and no training or hyperparameter search, GAR takes TRM from 85.9% to 99.4% on Sudoku-Extreme and from 68.8% to 85.6% on Pencil Puzzle Bench validation. On the same checkpoints, GAR also outperforms Probabilistic TRM (PTRM), which perturbs z at each step, even when PTRM uses 42 to 197 times as much compute.

title: ECHO: Correcting Time Series Foundation Model Forecasts with Historical Analogues and Errors
summary: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide general-purpose forecasting capabilities, yet their forecasts can remain misaligned with the temporal characteristics of a target domain. This motivates lightweight forecast correction even when only black-box access to the TSFM is available. Our key observation is that two forms of historical information provide complementary correction signals: historical analogues reveal how similar contexts evolved, while past forecast errors reveal a TSFM's characteristic deviations in the target domain. Based on this observation, we propose ECHO, a black-box forecast correction framework that learns from both sources. ECHO uses AnalogE to assess retrieved historical analogues together with the current context and base forecast, learning transferable corrections through cross-domain pretraining. In parallel, RecentE learns target-specific residual corrections from past forecast errors and refines them as causally available feedback accumulates. ECHO dynamically combines the two corrections according to their observed forecasting performance. Across 5 representative TSFMs and 9 real-world datasets, ECHO reduces MSE in all 45 backbone--dataset settings, yielding an average relative reduction of 9.26\% in macro-average MSE. Its gains also extend to long-horizon forecasting.

title: ARMED: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Medication Recommendation
summary: Medication recommendation requires jointly considering diagnoses, comorbidities, longitudinal patient history, and treatment interactions. Although recent retrieval-augmented generation approaches using language models have shown promise for clinical recommendation, most existing systems rely on fixed retrieval pipelines that cannot adapt to diverse clinical retrieval scenarios and may introduce noisy or irrelevant evidence. We propose ARMED, an adaptive clinical RAG framework that dynamically expands retrieval according to retrieval sufficiency and current-admission relevance. ARMED first observes the initial retrieval outcome and selectively performs supplementary or fallback multi-query retrieval when additional evidence is needed. The framework also incorporates a relevance gate that activates only clinically relevant same-patient history and organizes retrieved evidence into structured query-level clinical evidence. Experiments on MIMIC-IV demonstrate that ARMED consistently outperforms previous static retrieval baselines and improves overall medication recommendation quality. By combining locally runnable small language models with adaptive retrieval, ARMED supports medication recommendation without relying on external language model APIs or task-specific fine-tuning.

title: StructZO: Structured Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.

title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.

title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.

title: Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens: Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Systems
summary: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%--40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%--2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM's 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.

title: pi-Net: Empirical Latent Representations for Differentiable Physics Heads in Data-Scarce Systems
summary: Developing reliable predictive models for multi-physics systems often forces a compromise between computationally demanding physical simulators and data-hungry, opaque machine learning (ML) algorithms. While incorporating dimensional analysis into directed computation graphs offers a structurally sound alternative to explicitly solving partial differential equations (PDEs), such formulations typically yield underdetermined systems that act as imperfect simulators. We introduce pi-Net, a physics-informed latent variable model that resolves these imperfect simulators. The hybrid pi-Net architecture consists of an encoder that maps inputs into physically normalized latent space, which are then decoded into final predictions by a differentiable physics head. Evaluated on a real-world, data-scarce Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) case study, the framework achieves an R2 of 0.864 with only 60 experimental samples. The results demonstrate that pi-Net significantly outperforms purely data-driven baselines in data-scarce regimes while providing causal, process-level explainability.

title: Asymptotic Risk of Learning-Rate Schedules for Least-Squares Regression with Discretely Distributed Features
summary: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on streaming least squares with discretely distributed features (Slock's model), which decouples the dynamics across eigendirections. Under power-law source and capacity conditions, we derive the exact finite-time risk and asymptotic equivalents of constant and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedules. With a tuned base learning-rate, the resulting scaling law decays as $Θ(T^{-q})$, where $T$ is the horizon, and $q$ is independent of the cooldown length $c \in (0,1]$ but is strictly smaller for the constant schedule: any cooldown of fixed relative length $c > 0$, however short, improves the risk by a polynomial factor, while its length only affects the constant, which is minimized by linear decay ($c = 1$). Finally, we show that the optimal risk depends on the batch size $b$ and horizon $T$ only through $bT$, up to a critical batch size.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Hawkes-Structured Networks for Market Making
summary: Market making under realistic order-flow dynamics is challenging due to the clustered, self-exciting nature of order arrivals, which are naturally modeled by non-Markovian Hawkes processes. We propose a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) framework for market making with general Hawkes order-flow dynamics. We first establish non-asymptotic performance bounds that quantify the loss incurred by approximating the infinite-dimensional Hawkes state using a finite collection of exponentially weighted features. Guided by this analysis, we introduce the Hawkes-Structured Network (HSN), a novel neural architecture that encodes historical order flow through a learnable mixture-of-exponentials filter. HSN is trained end-to-end using model-free RL, jointly optimizing the feature representation and quoting policy directly from reward feedback. Experiments on single- and multi-asset market-making problems with mixture-of-exponentials, power-law, and regime-switching kernels demonstrate that HSN outperforms general-purpose neural architectures, achieving higher trading rewards while implicitly recovering the underlying order-flow intensities.

title: Learning Graded Sparse Mechanisms: A Representation Theorem and Certified Generalization
summary: In a variety of multi-agent and physical environments, an element's update depends strongly on a few other elements and weakly on many, and both the identity and the number of the elements that matter change with the state of the system. Such graded sparse mechanisms are common, for instance, in flocks, crowds, learned particle simulators and the neighborhood aggregation of graph networks, yet they have received little systematic study as a class of functions with the grading given. In this paper we study the supervised learning of the mechanism when the grading is provided by the environment, as a weight on every element. First, we define the class by axioms, where each element's influence is capped by its weight, the dependence on the weights is regular, and no element is distinguished, and prove a representation theorem: the class is exactly the Lipschitz ball of a transport metric on weighted multisets, and the metric is forced by the axioms. Next, the geometry of the representation gives generalization bounds that depend on the data in two ways. One is via the sparsity profile of the data -- the law of how many elements matter and by how much -- which bounds the rate over all designs with that profile, with an exponent from the profile and no dependence on the number of elements. In a number of natural cases we also show matching lower bounds, up to constants in the exponent. The other is empirical: due to the representation result, classical empirical discrepancy bounds apply to the class as they stand, and the resulting bound is the transport distance between the two halves of the sample in the class's own metric, computed exactly by a matching, with an additional concentration term. Finally, we study a simulated Vicsek flock under four interaction rules at two noise levels, and show that the certificate is non-vacuous, a small fraction of the trivial value on every rule.

title: DeepFlow: Two Convergent Differentiable Approaches for Pairwise Conditional Random Fields
summary: Basic probabilistic models form the basis of modern deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer of a network and allowing the networks outputs to be interpreted through a probabilistic lens. By increasing the complexity of these final activation layers to include features such as spatial regularisation, allow for these models to improve in performance without requiring significantly more data. The challenge however is to ensure that these more complex probabilistic graphical models adapt well to being used in tandem with deep learning, that is, ensuring they converge and have meaningful derivatives. The goal of this paper is to show two algorithms with provable convergence properties to allow this type of regularisation for image and signal classification models. Through both rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, we can show the differing performance between these solution types.

title: Optimal Transport PAC-Bayes Bounds
summary: PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds are among the strongest distribution-dependent guarantees in statistical learning and are typically expressed in terms of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between a prior and posterior distribution. While analytically convenient, the KL divergence requires the posterior to be absolutely continuous w.r.t. the prior, imposing support constraints that can substantially restrict the choice of posterior. Moreover, the KL divergence does not account for the underlying geometry of the probability space. In this work, we derive new PAC-Bayesian bounds replacing the KL divergence with general optimal transport (OT) distances, including the total variation and Wasserstein-$p$ distances.

title: The Language of Looking: Motion Tokens Reveal Domain-Dependent Local Structure in Gaze Sequences
summary: Human gaze is the primary high-bandwidth interface through which we parse the semantics of our environment. While often modeled as a sequence, the degree to which gaze exhibits transferable local structure across domains remains underexplored. Using motion tokenization as a diagnostic lens across four diverse datasets, we investigate the transferability of local sequence structure. We demonstrate that while gaze can share a reusable motion-token vocabulary, identical motion tokens are organized into different local transition patterns depending on the dataset and task context. Our results show the limitations of naive data-pooling under low-semantic motion-token representations and provide a framework for evaluating behavioral sequences through information-theoretic diagnostics.

title: Characterizing and Mitigating Distributional Bias in Physics-Informed Generative Models
summary: Physics-informed generative models augment a data-fitting objective with residual penalties that encourage physical constraints to hold in generated samples. However, improving constraint satisfaction need not improve fidelity to the data distribution. We study this conflict in residual-regularized diffusion models and identify two possible consequences. First, the same prediction error can incur different residual costs near different feasible states, preferring states with lower residual sensitivity (avoidance). Second, this preference can extend to feasible states outside the data support, where the residual also vanishes (leakage). Motivated by this analysis, we propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian at the clean training sample and normalizes the resulting magnitude. This removes the incentive to relocate to less sensitive states without changing the model architecture or sampling procedure. Experiments on a controlled synthetic system, three PDE systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching demonstrate the benefits of anchoring. Code is available at https://github.com/TanjaBien/anchored_diffusion.

title: OctMole: Multiscale 3D Molecular Generation with Hierarchical Spatial Flows
summary: Generating accurate 3D molecules requires jointly determining a variable number of atoms, their identities, and geometry across spatial scales: global shape emerges coarsely, whereas chemical bonds demand fine local precision. Existing atom-based diffusion and flow models operate largely at a single scale, while dense spatial fields become costly at high resolution. We introduce OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. A hierarchical occupancy flow progressively resolves sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, and a joint atom flow assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves. This decomposition combines efficient global structure with subcell geometric precision, while cell corruption improves robustness to generated support. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, OctMole achieves strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with particularly clear gains over Uni-3DAR on GEOM-DRUG and substantial efficiency gains over dense 3D generation. As an additional capability, intermediate occupancy states and selected regions provide spatial conditioning without task-specific retraining, supporting multiscale shape conditioning, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation. Code and pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/octree-nn/octmole and https://huggingface.co/Disembo/octmole, respectively.

title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.

title: Towards Modality-Agnostic Seizure Classification: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Heterogeneous EEG and Intracranial EEG Signals
summary: Seizure prediction and detection, essential for clinical treatment of epilepsy, remain the crucial task of this neurological disease. EEG and iEEG are widely used to analyze epilepsy due to its capability of capturing discriminative brain activities at high time resolution. However, existing works generally analyze either EEG or iEEG seizure activity separately, where EEG analysis has been well-researched, while more and more works consider iEEG for its higher specificity at the spatial level and signal quality. Currently, most of the existing seizure prediction systems are single-modal in nature, which limits its application to a variety of clinical conditions. Therefore, a common framework to analyze seizures with both EEG and iEEG signals needs to be developed. This paper presents a new framework of multimodal seizure classification integrating the heterogeneous EEG and iEEG recordings from different subjects and sources. A specific framework, called Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (UMSH), is developed for harmonizing signals with varied sampling rates and recording conditions. Moreover, to handle the extremely class-imbalanced problem in the data sets, we use a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) based data augmentation technique to generate synthetic samples to balance the class distribution. The proposed framework uses the EEGNet-Vision Transformer (EEGNet-ViT) as the feature extraction and classification network to learn the local discriminative patterns as well as global contextual information in the multimodal seizure data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for robust seizure classification, emphasizing the potential of integrated EEG-iEEG multimodal learning in advancing next-generation epilepsy monitoring and clinical decision-support systems.

title: DEFlow: Deep Equilibrium Flow Maximum-Entropy Reinforcement Learning
summary: Expressive flow policies can represent multiple high-value actions, but sampling them with few integration steps while retaining tractable action densities remains challenging. We introduce DEFlow, a deep equilibrium flow policy that replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as an equilibrium system. We combine implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density, enabling off-policy training within soft actor-critic without backpropagating through solver iterations. DEFlow achieves an average relative improvement of approximately 10% in mean successful coverage over the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants. It also achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, while remaining broadly competitive across five MuJoCo tasks. These results support implicit flow policies for tasks requiring both diversity and precision, at the cost of additional nonlinear and linear solves. Primary

title: DR-APO: Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization from Continuous Control to Embodied Navigation
summary: Policy representations in reinforcement learning have expanded beyond Gaussian policies to diffusion and flow-matching based generative policies. However, existing RL methods remain representation-specific, lacking a unified optimization interface for emerging generative policies. In particular, extending likelihood-based objectives to multi-step generative policies couples optimization to their internal generation process, where accumulated likelihood ratios can weaken the update signal. Meanwhile, generative-policy-specific methods often rely on multi-candidate generation and critic-based selection, improving overall return while providing limited improvement to the policy itself. We introduce DR-APO (Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization), which decouples policy improvement from policy representation through advantage-guided target improvement and representation-compatible direct action fitting, providing a shared optimization principle for Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies. Across five MuJoCo-v5 tasks, DR-APO remains competitive with SAC for Gaussian policies and achieves the best aggregate policy-only performance for both diffusion and flow-matching policies. NavDP post-training improves the Success Rate (SR) from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% in real-world navigation. These results demonstrate a unified policy-improvement principle across Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies, from continuous-control learning to embodied-policy post-training.

title: AeroChem: Closed-loop Physics-Informed State Space Modeling for Long-term Chemically-Reactive Air Quality Forecasting--Extended Version
comment: 25 pages. An extended version of "AeroChem: Closed-loop Physics-Informed State Space Modeling for Long-term Chemically-Reactive Air Quality Forecasting--Extended Version" accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Accurate long-term air quality forecasting is challenging due to long-range transport, meteorological variability, and nonlinear chemical reactions underlying secondary pollutant formation. Purely data-driven models often suffer from long-horizon drift and lack physical consistency, while existing physics-informed approaches commonly follow open-loop designs that fuse neural and physical components only at the output level. We propose AeroChem, a closed-loop physics-informed state space framework for chemically reactive air quality forecasting. AeroChem adopts a two-branch co-correction design: a UDE-based process branch provides a structured but imperfect physical prior, while a Mamba-based virtual measurement branch captures long-range temporal context and produces probabilistic virtual observations. Neural Kalman Fusion couples the two branches by correcting the latent physical state at each forecasting step and feeding the posterior state back into the simulator, reducing long-horizon drift. We further introduce HanoiAir, a real-world dataset integrating pollutant concentrations, meteorology, and emission inventories. Experiments on HanoiAir and a public benchmark show that AeroChem improves long-horizon stability and sudden-change forecasting.

title: ACED: Reference-Anchored Aggregation of Natural-Language and Executable Evidence for Mathematical Reasoning
comment: 23 pages, including references and appendices. Yiyi Lu and Jiaxiang Geng contributed equally
summary: Natural-language self-consistency and executable programs provide complementary test-time evidence for mathematical reasoning, yet either channel may support the same semantic error. Thus we propose ACED, a reference-anchored framework that treats the self-consistency answer as the default and executable outputs as supporting evidence rather than interchangeable votes. ACED converts source-specific answer counts into smoothed supports, combines them through a weighted logarithmic pool, and overrides the reference only when a calibrated relative-evidence margin is exceeded. The same rule supports both candidate selection and admission of executable-only answers. Across five math word-problem benchmarks, ACED matches or outperforms the corresponding baselines. On GSM8K, ACED-CANDIDATE recovers 89.7% of the attainable candidate-set gain with only three damaging overrides, while ACED-ALL reaches 86.9% accuracy versus 82.6% for direct Program-of-Thought aggregation. These results show that preserving evidence provenance enables more reliable integration of natural-language and executable reasoning.

title: Learning Deployable Causal Action Geometry under Temporal Non-Stationarity
summary: Learning a response law for continuous decisions from observational time series is central to many real-world decision systems, yet temporal non-stationarity poses a fundamental challenge: as outcomes drift over time, naively pooled models can conflate action effects with shifting baselines and even reverse action rankings. Even when the one-step response is identifiable, unrestricted cross-time generalization remains fundamentally ill-posed. We therefore seek the part of the response that remains stable for decisions even when outcome levels do not. We propose deployable causal action geometry: the action-response shape that remains after anchoring away action-independent level shifts on a selected link scale and profiling out positive amplitude variation. Building on this target, we develop a two-stage orthogonal estimator that first obtains cross-fitted pilot estimates of anchored responses and then performs honest profiled selection over link, representation, and shape classes. The resulting estimator admits oracle guarantees for the restricted target and, under approximate persistence, produces decision rules that remain near optimal in future periods. Experiments on synthetic data and Dominick's support the proposed target and its transfer behavior. In a randomized Taobao A/B test, the deployed system improves GMV and purchase counts by \(1.16\%\) and \(1.70\%\).

title: Learning Incompressible 3D Flows from Sparse Samples: A Set Transformer Approach to Divergence-Free Kernel Fitting
summary: Recovering divergence-free velocity fields from sparse and corrupted observations requires reconciling physical consistency, expressive representations, and robustness to missing data. We introduce DFK-Former, a set-to-field transformer that reconstructs divergence-free velocity fields from sparse, noisy, and irregularly sampled 3D observations. The model is inherently invariant to the number and ordering of input samples and predicts the parameters of a divergence-free kernel representation, producing continuous, mesh-free velocity fields that satisfy incompressibility exactly by construction rather than approximately through soft constraints or projection operators. Unlike existing divergence-free kernel approaches, which estimate kernel coefficients via a separate optimization for each field, DFK-Former predicts these coefficients directly in a single forward pass. This eliminates costly iterative fitting while providing a learned prior that enables accurate reconstruction even when observations are insufficient to uniquely determine the field. To enhance representational power, we introduce adaptive and anisotropic divergence-free kernels that preserve exact incompressibility guarantees while capturing more complex flow structures. Extensive experiments across varying levels of sparsity, noise, and occlusion, including transfer to real Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) turbulence data, demonstrate substantial gains in both accuracy and efficiency. DFK-Former reduces endpoint error by up to 4.6x compared to per-field divergence-free-kernel optimization, while reconstructing each field in 7.5 ms instead of 9.8 s, yielding a speedup of more than three orders of magnitude. These results establish direct, feed-forward prediction of divergence-free kernel parameters as a practical and effective paradigm for physically consistent velocity-field reconstruction from sparse observations.

title: IND-Eval: Aligning Evaluation and Simulation for Industrial Time Series Foundation Models
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the Foundation Models for Temporal Systems workshop at NeurIPS 2026. IND-Eval: https://huggingface.co/datasets/cognitedata/IND-eval
summary: We introduce IND-Eval, a public benchmark that organizes industrial time series across domains into source-specific forecasting tasks. Relative to established benchmarks such as GIFT-Eval, it emphasizes finer sampling resolutions and a greater prevalence of multivariate forecasting. Evaluating Chronos-2, TiRex-2, and TimesFM-3, we find that TimesFM-3 achieves the lowest source-balanced aggregate nMASE and nCRPS and leads seven of nine sources under each metric; source-specific exceptions reinforce the need for domain-representative evaluation for model selection. These findings also motivate improving domain alignment during pretraining, where real industrial data are often too scarce to close domain-specific gaps directly; we therefore investigate whether a domain's statistical structure can guide simulator design. In a case study on two offshore well-monitoring regimes, we improve a general simulator's coverage using an oscillator-augmented simulation pipeline. This lowers forecasting error in the target domain but reduces performance on the subset of GIFT-Eval with natively univariate targets. A 50/50 mixture of the general and augmented simulation recipes achieves the lowest error among the three training recipes for all four event-metric pairs in the case study while recovering most of the lost GIFT-Eval performance. Together, these results illustrate how domain-representative evaluation can guide model selection and the composition of simulated data while revealing a trade-off between specialization and generality.

title: Counting with Attention and LayerNorm: Norm Scaling and Representation Geometry
summary: Counting is a simple task on which transformers can nevertheless fail at long sequence lengths. We study the cost of counting in a single attention layer, up to a maximum length $L$, focusing on how softmax attention and layer normalization shape the representation from which the count is recovered. We mainly focus on regression read-out but also consider classification read-out. For regression, we show unnormalized linear attention counts exactly at parameter norms independent of $L$. For softmax attention, regression cannot count exactly with finite parameters; it recovers the count after rounding, but only when the vector parameter norms grow with $L$. We measure this cost by $B_{\min}$, the smallest bound that can be placed on every trainable vector to ensure exact counting after rounding, and derive tight rates. At fixed model dimension, $B_{\min}$ grows as $L$ without normalization, as $L^{3/2}$ under bare post-normalization, and as $L^{3/4}$ with learned post-normalization. The last rate is unexpected: post-normalization discards the magnitude that carries the count and might be expected to make counting harder, yet with a learnable gain it counts at a smaller norm than softmax without normalization. Bare pre-normalization is different: it bounds the attention scores, so beyond a finite length no parameter norm suffices. A classification read-out keeps every norm bounded under every placement, but a dense head stores one output vector per count and costs more in storage. Experiments on the post-normalized model reproduce this split between the two read-outs. Together, our theoretical and empirical findings characterize how self-attention, layer-normalization placement, and read-out choice shape the representation geometry and parameter cost of counting in the minimal single-head architecture studied here.

title: Guidance Without Labels: Flow Matching from Coupled Gaussian Mixtures
summary: Flow matching models are typically trained to transport a Gaussian source to the data distribution, with source and target samples paired independently. We replace the source with a fitted Gaussian mixture and couple each data point to a mixture component through an entropic optimal transport problem. We show that the resulting transport reduces to the standard Gaussian-source problem up to a guidance-like correction, which enables the reuse of a pretrained velocity field. This correction is a closed-form function of the fitted mixture plus a term that we learn with a small correction network. We test our model on published checkpoints for CIFAR-10 and CelebA-HQ. It improves FID at every step count, and on CelebA-HQ it reaches the quality of the baseline with about half the steps. The closed-form term alone, with no training, already delivers most of this improvement; the small correction network accounts for the rest.

title: Compression Through Time: An Interplay of Separability, Stationarity and Capacity
summary: Information-theoretic and geometric compression have been widely studied as possible explanations for generalization. Yet their temporal dynamics in recurrent networks remain largely unexplored. Using discretized LSTMs, whose finite embedding space enables direct estimates of information quantities, we observe pronounced compression across the final timesteps of many datasets. We explain this effect through three competing mechanisms: (i) class separability permits stronger compression at the final timestep; (ii) shared recurrent dynamics propagate this pressure across timesteps with similar activation states, making its extent depend on temporal stationarity; and (iii) limited representational capacity opposes prolonged compression because it restricts information available for subsequent computation. We systematically test these mechanisms through controlled synthetic interventions and real-world sequence tasks. Our results identify class separability, temporal stationarity, and network capacity as key determinants of temporal compression, and suggest that compression acts as a regularizer-potentially beneficial when excess capacity is available, but harmful to generalization when it consumes memory needed for the task.

title: Making LoRA Identifiable: Orthogonal Alignment for Continual Learning
summary: There is growing interest in applying Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) to Continual Learning, as it enables faster training, mitigates catastrophic forgetting, and facilitates better adaptation to new tasks. Prior approaches have explored a range of strategies, including extending new LoRA branches for each incoming task, training under orthogonal loss objectives across all task-specific LoRA modules, and employing gating mechanisms to integrate new and existing LoRA modules. However, these methods incur memory costs that grow linearly with the number of tasks, limiting their scalability. More recent approaches investigate training a single LoRA by leveraging asymmetries in its parameterization; however, they often suffer from insufficient representational alignment across the LoRA parameter space. To address these limitations, we propose Stiefel Optimization and Aligned Rotation (SOAR), a two-stage framework for continual LoRA learning. First, we constrain the A matrix to lie on the Stiefel manifold, thereby reducing coordinate misalignment to the space of orthogonal rotation matrices. Second, we introduce an Orthogonal Procrustes alignment procedure for the B matrix to estimate the optimal rotation, coupled with a per-rank retention merging strategy that quantifies directional agreement between representations of new and previously learned tasks. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks, demonstrating that SOAR achieves strong continual learning performance without incurring additional memory overhead.

title: Feature-Context Consistency: Unsupervised Adversarial Detection with Drift Stability on Attributed Graphs
summary: Adversarial detection on evolving attributed graphs faces two challenges: fraud labels arrive late or not at all, and natural distributional drift erodes any trained decision boundary. Modern detectors can reach strong detection rates when labels are available and the distribution is stationary; sustaining that quality without labels and under drift is the open problem. We identify feature-context consistency -- the alignment between a node's attributes and its aggregated neighborhood attributes -- as a single structural signal that addresses both. We formalize it as the Context Boost (CB) score within a Restricted Boltzmann Machine framework (CB-RBM) and prove two complementary worst-case guarantees: a strict separation between the expected CB of legitimate and adversarial nodes, with gap growing linearly in model capacity, whenever the adversary's context stays far enough from legitimate neighborhood context; and a Wasserstein-Lipschitz bound on how far the CB distribution moves under natural drift. We validate on XBlock Ethereum phishing (~153K nodes) and Reddit banned-user detection (~11K nodes), with two further datasets in the appendix spanning diverse domains. With zero labels, CB-RBM achieves AUROC >= 0.96 on four adversarial attacks and keeps FPR close to its calibrated 5% target under drift -- outperforming supervised GNNs (hundreds of labels), unsupervised graph-anomaly baselines, and a standard RBM whose FPR collapses to 89-100%. What typically requires separate mechanisms -- label-free operation and drift stability -- here follows from a single structural regularity of the data. Code: https://github.com/serval-uni-lu/CB-RBM.

title: Attention-Graph Curvature for the Verification of Mathematical Reasoning
comment: Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI), NeurIPS 2026
summary: Language models have recently solved open Erdős problems and achieved gold-medal level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. But their solutions, written in natural language, cannot yet be verified by proof assistants. An erroneous reasoning step can invalidate every step that comes after, so it is advantageous to detect errors early. Several methods have been proposed to detect erroneous reasoning quickly based on the features of the forward pass of the language model that performs reasoning. In this work, we study whether the directed Forman curvature of that model's attention graph, a local quantity computed at an edge from the attention weights around it, carries information about a step's correctness. To do so, we evaluate four per-step verifiers on ProcessBench with and without the curvature appended to their input. Appending curvature values improves the overall mean performance of all four verifiers. ReProbe, the verifier that takes every token of a step as input, shows the largest improvement. Adding the curvature increases the time of the language model's forward pass by 18% on average.

title: Learn from Move: the Next Step for GUI Agents
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/ti-mm/LearnFromMove ; Benchmark and training data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/LatentGUIWorld
summary: Existing benchmarks for GUI agents primarily focus on increasing task difficulty by extending task horizons. Besides, enabling agents to explore unfamiliar environments and successfully complete tasks within them is also a critical yet challenging problem. We introduce LatentGUIWorld, a benchmark of six tasks in three matched pairs organized by the evidence needed for control: $I_0$ uses prior knowledge and available observations, $I_1$ requires interaction that directly reveals hidden semantics, and $I_2$ identifies dynamics from action-response relationships. Frontier models struggle especially on $I_2$ tasks. We introduce MOVE, which separates movement from button events and exposes intermediate visual feedback, together with demonstrations of iterative exploration and control. Ablations show that both action granularity and multi-step demonstrations improve performance. After SFT, LatentLearner-9B achieves 50.0% overall success on LatentGUIWorld, comparable to several frontier models. Joint RL further raises egocentric Drag and Ten-Choice success to 92.0% and 75.3%. Behavioral analysis reveals multi-step exploration. In egocentric Drag, RL increases Pearson correlation between error-normalized commands and ideal gain compensation from 0.610 to 0.803. Together, these behaviors show that models learn to explore through interaction and adapt their control to environment dynamics. The same format improves GUI grounding after RL, reaching 67.37% mean accuracy across five benchmarks versus 66.72% for conventional RL.

title: Before Attention Sinks Form: Hidden-State Geometry Reveals and Modulates Their Formation
summary: Attention sinks are usually studied after they have formed. We ask whether a measurable hidden-state change appears beforehand and whether changing that geometry alters what happens later. To remove network depth as a shortcut, we compare prompts in the same model and at the same layer. When sink timing varies across prompts, simple spectral summaries of the hidden states add information beyond current attention, with the clearest prompt-specific signal in a short window about two to three layers before sink formation. The predictive strength varies across cohorts, so we treat the spectrum as a readout of a pre-sink state change rather than a universal warning statistic. The signal is broader than one measured extreme activation. We then modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden states after current attention has already been computed. These interventions change later sink behavior in Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations. In Qwen2.5, the immediate suppressive effect is accompanied by a reduction in next-layer query--key preference for position~0, and the learned spectral directions remain stable when estimated from substantially less training data. Together, the results show that attention sinks are preceded by a short spectral reorganization of hidden states, and directly perturbing this geometry can causally alter subsequent sink formation.

title: NFMap: Topographic 2D Manifold Learning with Invertible Normalizing Flows
summary: We present NFMap, a dimensionality reduction method for 2D visualisation that extends Generative Topographic Mapping (GTM) with a bijective normalizing flow.
