The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

title: Depth Memory
summary: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.

title: Statistical Vignettes on the Grokking Phenomenon
summary: In this work, we study grokking in a simple, analytically tractable setting whose rich phenomenology allows us to disentangle the effects of initialization, signal strength, weight decay, sample size, and input dimension. These factors can produce superficially similar learning curves through distinct mechanisms, complicating their interpretation. Our analysis distinguishes early fitting through nuisance features, core feature learning, and delayed generalization. We identify sharp conditions under which grokking provably occurs and derive analytic asymptotic expressions for the lengths of the generalization plateaus. Our results also characterize regimes of early generalization and failure to reach a prescribed test accuracy target. We show that the interpolation edge constitutes a distinct dynamical regime, where vanishing spectral gaps separate core learning from generalization, helping clarify the role of proximity to interpolation in existing accounts of grokking. The resulting picture is analogous to fast and slow phases in chemical kinetics and suggests that the lazy-to-rich transition discussed in the literature may reflect a similar separation of dynamical time scales. Our theoretical results are faithfully supported by extensive experiments.

title: Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching
summary: A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness (Tong et al., 2024). However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance.

title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization
summary: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.

title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
summary: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

title: Bias Robustness of Genetic Multi-Criteria Sorting versus Learned Rankers under Proxy Skew and Label Contamination
summary: Learning-to-rank (LTR) models can align rankings with undesignated signals when those signals appear as features or leak into training labels. We compare label-free genetic multi-criteria sorting (open Pikaia strategy variants), which reranks fixed candidate pools using an explicit criteria vector C, to label-trained LTR (LightGBM, XGBoost, RankSVM) under two controlled protocols on MSLR-WEB10K, Baidu-ULTR, WANDS, and Expedia. In the main proxy-skew study, labels remain clean while a calibrated proxy P is available as a feature: Genetic AI rankings show lower Spearman rank-proxy correlation than the LTR peers (e.g. about 0.15-0.16 vs. 0.59-0.87 on WANDS), with both families evaluated jointly on clean nDCG@10 on a bias-utility frontier. In a supporting label-contamination study, training labels are mixed with contaminant B: because Genetic AI methods do not use labels, their bias and utility curves stay flat, whereas LightGBM and XGBoost increase rank-B correlation as contamination rises (OLS bias_slope about 0.58-0.65 on WANDS/Baidu). The results support genetic sorting as an architectural option for optimizing declared attributes on a fixed pool when undesignated proxies or label contaminants must be refused.

title: naspaclust: A hybridisation of spatial fuzzy clustering with nature-inspired optimisation
summary: We present an overview of R package called \texttt{naspaclust}, a tool for spatial fuzzy clustering improvement by hybridising the Fuzzy Geographically Weighted Clustering (FGWC) with nature-inspired optimisation algorithms. There are seven optimisation algorithms in general, namely Artificial Bee Colony, Flower Pollination Algorithm, Gravitational Search Algorithm, Harris-Hawk Optimisation, Intelligent Firefly Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimisation, and Teaching-Learning Based optimisation. The optimisation algorithms available do not only use the basic algorithms, but also the modified version of several parts such as randomisation terms and updating rules. Furthermore, we also provide additional options by providing more distance metrics options based on the \texttt{ rdist} package. This study showed the implementation of the \texttt{naspaclust} package in various cases, as well as comparing the performance of the algorithms in the scope of basic algorithms. The \texttt{naspaclust} package allows to improve the performance of fuzzy clustering, mainly in spatial context.

title: Time Window Optimization for Motor Imagery Classification via Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Code available at https://github.com/LunaLab-XJTU/TSE-RL
summary: Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) typically decode continuous EEG using fixed-length sliding windows that may be misaligned with neural events. Existing window optimization methods often evaluate windows independently, overlooking temporal dependencies and potentially producing fragmented or physiologically implausible selections. We propose Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning (TSE-RL), a framework that incorporates prior knowledge of MI event structure into a constrained Markov decision process for adaptive window optimization. First, TSE-RL assigns each window an explicit semantic role through Discard, Onset, Sustain, or Offset actions, extending binary retain/discard decisions to event-level alignment. Second, a finite-state machine masks invalid actions to enforce the temporal order of MI phases and promote physiologically plausible window sequences. Third, a Transformer-based history encoder captures dependencies across windows, improving training stability and computational efficiency compared with recurrent architectures. TSE-RL is plug-and-play and can be integrated with diverse MI classifiers. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in decoding performance in both cross-session and cross-subject settings. Visualization analyses further suggest that the learned window selection policy aligns with neurophysiological principles.

title: Criticality-related dynamics accompany long-term functional decline in primary cortical MEA cultures
summary: Primary cortical neuron cultures are widely used to study network development and decline, but their long-term electrophysiological trajectories are poorly characterized. We used multi-electrode arrays to longitudinally monitor Wistar rat cortical cultures for up to ~730 days in vitro (DIV), combining activity measures with survival analysis and criticality metrics. Wells shared an early developmental phase, with mean firing rate peaking at 12-14 Hz around DIV 100-150, before diverging into two phenotypes: early-death wells, showing progressive loss of burst organization, longer inter-burst intervals, shorter bursts, and steep declines in active-electrode recruitment; and long-survival wells, which sustained organized bursting and measurable activity well beyond DIV 400, in some cases past DIV 700. Cox proportional-hazards modeling with FDR correction across thirteen candidate features identified burst duration, inter-burst interval, synchrony, mean firing rate, branching ratio, and Kappa index as significant predictors of time to network failure. Criticality metrics offered the most mechanistic insight: in early-death wells, branching ratio declined toward zero and Kappa index rose toward its upper bound as networks approached silencing. Beyond their average levels, the rate of change of branching ratio and Kappa index over recordings was the strongest correlate of survival time among all criticality metrics. Neuronal avalanche size and duration exponents and their scaling relation, remained consistent with scale-free dynamics in both phenotypes while networks were active, though avalanche occurrence rate declined progressively in early-death wells without reaching significance as an independent predictor. These results show that long-term network survival is not determined by firing rate alone, but by preserved burst organization, sustained electrode recruitment and near-critical propagation dynamics. This work offers one of the longest electrophysiological characterizations of rodent cortical cultures to date and identifies criticality-based metrics as promising tools for predicting network decline and evaluating interventions to preserve long-term neuronal function.

title: Neurite Complexity and Plasticity Markers Track Synaptic Vesicle Density in the Living Human Brain: A Multimodal PET-MRI-EEG Study
summary: Neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganise its structure and function, is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases and a putative mechanism of action for pharmacological interventions. [11C]-UCBJ positron emission tomography (PET), which quantifies synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) density, offers the most direct in vivo measure of human synaptic density, but its relationship to complementary, more scalable neuroimaging measures of structural and functional plasticity remains uncharacterised. We combined [11C]-UCBJ PET, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI/NODDI), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG)-based sensory tasks (roving mismatch negativity, MMN; visual long-term potentiation, vLTP) in 18 healthy volunteers to test the relationship between synaptic terminal SV2A density and complementary structural and functional neuroplasticity measures, and whether these relationships were reproducible following pharmacological challenge with ketamine (n = 11) or N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT; n = 7). There were no statistically significant differences in PET-derived SV2A binding potential (BPND), DWI-derived neurite orientation dispersion (ODI) and structural weighted degree (SWD), EEG-derived MMN repetition suppression, and late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation, 1 to 8 days following DMT and ketamine exposure compared to baseline. BPND was coupled with ODI across cortical regions before and after pharmacological challenge, and this relationship was tighter within visual, attentional, and frontoparietal control brain networks. SWD showed a weaker, more spatially restricted association with BPND, primarily in regions belonging to the limbic and visual brain networks, but was not replicated post-drug. No consistent association was found between BPND and functional weighted degree (FWD), derived from rs-fMRI, at baseline or after pharmacological challenge. Frontotemporal BPND was positively associated with MMN repetition suppression (r = 0.61), and occipital BPND with late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation (r = 0.54), with the MMN-BPND association replicating after pharmacological challenge (r = 0.49). These findings link synaptic terminal SV2A density in the living human brain to neurite architecture and the capacity for short-term and Hebbian-like long-term synaptic plasticity, while dissociating these relationships from generic functional connectivity and magnitude of sensory-evoked responses. These data provide cross-modal validation for DWI- and EEG-derived measures as biological indices and surrogate measures of human synaptic plasticity.

title: Adaptive co-transmission shapes sensory encoding and behavior
summary: Co-transmission expands the chemical repertoire of neurons, but whether coexisting neurotransmitters can be independently organized and remodeled by experience to control distinct aspects of behavior remains unclear. Here, we address this question in the AFD thermosensory neuron of Caenorhabditis elegans, which directs navigation toward a learned temperature preference. We find that glutamatergic and cholinergic vesicular transporters coexist within individual presynaptic boutons but differ in axonal trafficking, subsynaptic organization, and dependence on presynaptic machinery. Sensory experience differentially regulates the two systems: animals trained to prefer higher temperatures exhibit increased VGLUT/EAT-4 abundance, whereas those trained to prefer lower temperatures exhibit increased VAChT/UNC-17 abundance. The two transmitters also make distinct, context-dependent contributions to goal-directed navigation. Glutamatergic transmission promotes movement toward the learned thermal preference, whereas cholinergic transmission restrains continued migration beyond it. Analysis of locomotor trajectories further reveals that the two transmitters differentially regulate reorientation decisions across regions of the thermal gradient. Together, these findings identify adaptive co-transmission, a form of synaptic plasticity in which coexisting neurotransmitter systems are differentially organized and regulated by experience, and make distinct, context-dependent contributions to behavior.

title: Scan field rotation with a K-mirror for fast two-photon imaging along curved planes
summary: In contrast to the curved geometry of biological structures, the imaging plane of conventional microscopes is flat. In principle, axial scanning can adjust the focus to follow curved structures. In resonant scanning microscopes, which are broadly used for video-rate functional imaging, however, such focus adjustment is typically possible at rates faster than the slow (~30 Hz) scan axis but not as fast as the fast (~8000 Hz) resonant axis. The fixed direction of the fast resonant axis therefore constrains how the imaging plane can be tilted or curved using axial scanning, and limits how well it can be aligned with biological structures of interest. Here, we present an optical modification that overcomes this constraint. Specifically, we combine scan field rotation using a K-mirror with fast axial scanning using an electrically tunable lens. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach for calcium imaging by aligning the imaging plane with the curved pyramidal cell layer in mouse hippocampus, increasing the number of simultaneously imaged neurons. In addition, we image dendritic arbors of hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons that would otherwise be only partially accessible for fast imaging, and we apply our method to the curved layers of cerebellar Purkinje cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate how scan field rotation can be used to optimally orient a dendritic branch for high-speed subcellular glutamate imaging. Our approach is based on a single module and can therefore be retrofitted to standard two-photon systems. We openly share design specifications, 3D-printed parts, and custom ScanImage-compatible code to facilitate rapid adoption.

title: Trigeminal Nerve Stimulation Attenuates Traumatic Brain Injury-Induced Neuronal Damage via CGRP-PINK1 Mitophagy Axis
summary: Secondary damage after traumatic brain injury (TBI) is driven by progressive mitochondrial failure, yet clinically viable strategies to directly safeguard mitochondrial networks remain a major therapeutic gap. Here, we show that non-invasive trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS), which engages the brain's endogenous oxygen-conserving diving reflex, preserves neuronal survival by directly regulating the mitochondrial PINK1/Parkin quality-control pathway. We demonstrate that TBI induces the pathological aggregation of the outer mitochondrial membrane receptor TOM20, in a CGRP-dependent manner, which affects binding of the damage-sensor PINK1 and renders downstream Parkin-mediated rescue ineffective. TNS-induced neuronal CGRP release prevents this TOM20 aggregation, restoring proper PINK1 function and downstream Parkin activation. This preservation of mitochondrial architecture reinforces the outer membrane's barrier function, limiting pro-apoptotic cytochrome c leakage and supporting NRF2 antioxidant defenses, ultimately reducing progressive infarct expansion and recovering sensorimotor functions. The significance of this work lies in bridging physical neuromodulation directly to the preservation of organelle-level architecture. By demonstrating that stimulation of trigeminal afferents to recruit an oxygen-conserving reflex can stabilize outer membrane signaling architecture and preserve mitochondrial survival machinery, this study outlines a non-pharmacological strategy to protect mitochondrial function and inhibit acute post-traumatic neurodegeneration.

title: A Reproducible Cortical Model of Focal Epileptiform Activity with a Multi-Biomarker Analysis Pipeline
summary: The development of surface-based therapeutic strategies, including extracranial illumination and epicortical electrical or optoelectronic neuromodulation, requires experimental models in which focal pathological activity can be generated and monitored within an accessible cortical region. Here, we established an acute cortical model of focal epileptiform activity in anesthetized mice based on local microinjection of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) into the barrel cortex. This preparation provides precise spatial and temporal control of the epileptiform focus while enabling simultaneous electrophysiological sampling across cortical depth. To objectively characterize the induced activity, we implemented a Python-based analysis pipeline integrating complementary electrophysiological biomarkers, including oscillatory power, multi-unit activity, pathological fast ripples (250-650 Hz), and epileptiform bursts. Local 4-AP administration produced robust increases in gamma (30-100 Hz) power, multi-unit firing (MUA), fast ripple and burst activity. Pharmacological sensitivity of the framework was evaluated using carbamazepine, which robustly attenuated 4-AP-induced increases in all biomarkers. Together, this study provides a reproducible experimental and analytical framework for investigating focal cortical epileptiform activity and for the future evaluation of pharmacological, optical, and electrical interventions targeting superficial cortical networks.

title: Differential subcortical-cortical circuit reorganization in autism and ADHD
summary: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often co-occur and share symptoms as well as genetic risk factors. While subcortical-cortical networks have been implicated in both conditions, particularly involving thalamic and striatal circuits, patterns of shared and diverging disruptions remain unclear. Here we integrated resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and regression dynamic causal modeling (rDCM) across a transdiagnostic multi-site cohort. We used statistical group comparisons and individualized normative deviation mapping to map network deviations in ASD and ADHD relative to neurotypical controls and against one another. Multivariate associative techniques examined associations to clinical and cognitive phenotypes. Our transdiagnostic analyses revealed significant differentiation of ASD and ADHD across subcortical-cortical circuits. While ASD was characterized by widespread thalamocortical hyperconnectivity and bidirectional elevated coupling across thalamic subdivisions, ADHD exhibited a focal pattern of striatocortical disruption, anchored predominantly within the caudate. Multivariate analyses identified shared and disorder-specific brain-behavior associations. Across both conditions, aberrant striatocortical signaling was associated with reduced overall intelligence measures. Clinically, ASD-related thalamocortical connectivity disruptions mapped onto generalized cognitive impairment, whereas ADHD-related subcortical alterations tracked hyperactive and inattentive symptom dimensions. Our findings differentiate ASD and ADHD through distinct patterns of functional and directional subcortical-cortical dysregulations.
